evidence_summary: Mica-Tone appears in East Coast Fuzz research as a marketed identity associated with the Manny's/Orpheum/Clark cluster, but the name also appears on a separate Japanese FY-6 Super-Fuzz-derived product. The archive must keep these as distinct identity records until enclosure, labeling, date, and construction evidence proves continuity.

Effects Database describes Mica-Tone Fuzz Master as one of the rebranded FY-6 Super-Fuzz versions made by a Japanese OEM. This record must remain separate from the East Coast Mica-Tone candidate because the identical brand name does not establish a common manufacturer or product lineage.

A surviving Tim's Own Fuzzer Buzzer is marketed as a 1968 example with period pot dates, and collector evidence groups it with Manny's, Clark, Wurlitzer and Orpheum forms. This confirms chronology and family identity more strongly than the previous entry, but still does not identify a physical factory.

A surviving E.U. Wurlitzer Fuzzer Buzzer carries CTS-style pot code 1376728, decoding to the 20th week of 1967. The source confirms the physical existence and chronology of the marketed state, while its seller attribution to Apollo/Orpheum Japanese production remains unverified and is excluded from builder claims.

Gene Andre's New Jersey electronics background and closely related reverb, mixer, amp and tremolo construction make him a meaningful builder hypothesis, but the current evidence still supports only a candidate relationship. No direct period document tying Andre Audio-Tronics to the East Coast Fuzz production run was found in this pass.

Effects Database groups a Halifax Fuzz with the Clark SS-600, E.U. Wurlitzer and MGI two-knob forms. The current source set does not establish whether Halifax was a retailer, a distributor, or a separate production label, so no factory attribution is promoted.
